subject: Canada's counter-tariffs hit 700 U.S. goods at 12:01 a.m.
bodyMarkdown:
The counter-tariffs Ottawa announced two weeks ago stopped being a plan at 12:01 this morning. If you buy groceries or run a business that brings anything in from the States, today is when the trade war turns into a number on your invoice.

## What is on the list

Canada put tariffs of 15, 25 and 50 per cent on more than 700 American products at 12:01 a.m. eastern, matching Washington rate for rate on the same goods. Al Jazeera reported this morning that the list covers close to $20 billion of imports, spread across steel and aluminum, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, plastics, seafood, clothing and electronics. The 50 per cent band doubles the rate on American steel and aluminum from 25 per cent. All of it answers **Section 338**, a clause of the 1930 U.S. Tariff Act that lets a president hit countries he says discriminate against American commerce, and the law firm White & Case wrote that Donald Trump's July proclamations were the first time any president had used it. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, announcing the list on August 25, called it "an unprecedented challenge imposed on Canada" and said "Canada will meet the moment."

## The fine print that decides who pays

Two details matter more than the headline rate. Goods already in transit to Canada when the clock struck are not charged, so importers who loaded containers last week get a pass, and the price effect will reach shelves in waves through October rather than today. Ottawa also says it intends to extend the existing United States Surtax Remission Order to the new list, subject to cabinet approval. **Remission** is the process where a company applies to have a duty waived because it cannot buy the input anywhere else, and company-specific relief already granted is expected to carry over. Cars are the other gap. Canada left its existing tariff on American vehicles alone and added nothing new, though trailers and semi-trailers got caught. Ottawa is still trying not to snap the auto supply chain it shares with Michigan and Ohio.

## The cheque Ottawa is writing today

The other thing landing today is money. The federal government is adding $1.5 billion to the Regional Tariff Response Initiative, the program its regional development agencies use to pay tariff-hit small and medium businesses, which brings it to $3.45 billion over four years. The rules for the expanded version are due to be published today. A business can get up to $3 million, made up of as much as $1 million for an investment or pivot project and as much as $2 million for liquidity, which is the new piece. To qualify, a firm has to have been viable before the tariffs and pull in at least $1 million in annual revenue. That revenue floor leaves out a lot of the smallest shops on Yonge Street, and I expect that to be the loudest complaint this week.

## The takeaway

The Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent on September 2 for the seventh straight decision and said inflation risks lean upward, naming the new tariffs as one reason, so nobody should count on the October 28 meeting to soften any of this. If you import American steel, dairy, appliances or electronics, find out today whether your goods cleared the border before 12:01 and whether you already hold a remission, because those two answers move your landed cost more than anything else will. Shoppers will feel it in October, not this week. I am watching the Regional Tariff Response Initiative rules when they post today, to see how many Canadian firms that $1 million revenue floor quietly shuts out.
